notes.b: Differences in participation are best understood through gender, the social side of being male or female, rather than through biology alone. So the first step is to separate the two words, which are often used as if they meant the same thing.
points: Sex: the biological characteristics, such as chromosomes (the genetic material that helps determine sex), hormones (chemical messengers in the body) and physical make-up, that define a person as male or female.
Gender: the socially constructed roles, behaviours and expectations (in other words, ideas made by society, not by biology) that a society attaches to being male or female.
Gender expectations differ between societies and change over time, so the activities seen as suitable for each sex are social rather than fixed.
Gendered activities: physical activities that a society labels as suitable for boys or for girls, for example rugby as 'for boys' and dance as 'for girls'.
notes.tip: Do not explain participation differences by biology alone. The specification frames them as social, so build your answer around gender.

notes.h: Participation patterns: how much, which activities and when drop-out happens
notes.b: Boys and girls do not take part in physical activity in the same way. The differences show up in how much they do, which activities they choose and when they stop, and they are described here in words, not percentages.
points: How much: on average, girls are less active than boys in physical activity and sport.
When: girls drop out of sport in greater numbers than boys during adolescence (the teenage years), especially in the senior cycle years (the last three years of secondary school).
Which activities: boys more often play competitive team and contact sports (where players physically tackle or collide), such as rugby and Gaelic football.
Which activities: girls more often choose dance, gymnastics, individual fitness and non-contact activities (where players do not tackle or collide).
Many activities are labelled 'for boys' or 'for girls', which steers young people towards the activities seen as suitable for their gender.
Participation changes across the life course (the stages of life from childhood to older age) and is shaped by many interacting influences rather than by biology alone.
notes.tip: Do not quote survey percentages, including ones you remember from past papers. Describe the pattern in words, such as 'girls are on average less active'.

notes.b: The family is the first place a child meets sport, and parents control much of what a child can try. Their attitudes can push boys and girls towards different activities.
points: Parents' own activity and encouragement shape whether a child sees physical activity as normal.
Parents decide what they will pay for and drive their children to, which controls access to clubs, coaching and training.
For boys: parents may encourage sons into contact sports and competitive team games.
For girls: parents may steer daughters towards activities they consider suitable, such as dance or gymnastics.
Example: a parent pays a son's club fees and drives him to matches, while a daughter's wish to join the same club is not supported.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to examine the main influences, so for each one say how it works, its effect on boys, its effect on girls and give an example.

notes.b: Peers (friends and classmates of the same age) matter most in the teenage years, when fitting in feels important. What friends think of sport can decide whether a young person takes part.
points: Friends' choices can decide whether a young person joins an activity or stays in it.
Fear of being judged by peers stops young people trying new activities.
For teenage girls: being sporty may be seen as uncool, so girls may downplay their interest in sport to fit in with friends.
For boys: sport can be central to status among peers, so skill in team sports can bring respect, while boys who are not sporty may lose standing.
notes.tip: Describing two influences on boys is a Higher question, so know the boys' side of peers as well as the girls' side.

notes.b: School is where most young people do most of their organised sport, so what a school offers and how it runs PE can widen or narrow the gender gap.
points: The range of activities offered often centres on competitive team games, which draw boys more than girls.
For girls: a narrow range of activities leaves those who prefer non-contact or individual activities with little to choose from.
For boys: competitive team games give boys a visible route into school teams and inter-school competition (matches between schools).
PE kit and changing facilities can deter girls where changing space is shared, poorly kept or lacks privacy.
Teacher expectations and attention: boys' teams often receive more of the teacher's time, and teachers may hold different expectations of girls' competitiveness.
Timetabling decides which activities run and when, so a fixed timetable can limit the choices open to each group.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how a school could tackle a gender imbalance, so use these causes to pick your solutions: each school influence has a matching fix in the school action block below.

notes.b: Outside school, whether a young person can play depends on what local clubs and facilities offer and on who they see succeeding in sport.
points: Provision: the teams, coaches, facility time and fixtures (scheduled matches) that let people take part, and how much of each is on offer.
For boys: boys often have more teams, better facility slots and more fixtures, so they can train and play more regularly.
For girls: fewer teams, coaches and facility slots limit how regularly they can train and play.
Role models: fewer visible female athletes, coaches and administrators (people who run clubs and governing bodies) mean girls see fewer people like themselves in sport and its leadership.
For boys: male role models dominate many visible team and contact sports, which reinforces the view that these sports belong to boys.

notes.b: What young people have to wear for an activity can decide whether they take part. Kit that shows the body can make teenagers, who are already conscious of how they look, want to avoid it.
points: Tight, short or revealing kit, such as swimwear, leotards, athletics briefs and short skirts, can make teenagers self-conscious about their bodies.
For girls: self-consciousness about kit can lead to avoiding an activity or dropping out, especially in adolescence.
For boys: tight or revealing kit can produce the same self-consciousness, leading some boys to avoid the activity too.
Comfortable kit that students can choose helps young people take part without feeling exposed.
notes.tip: An Ordinary Level question asks how required clothing can affect participation in certain sports. Name the kit, say it makes people self-conscious and say that leads to avoiding or dropping out.

notes.b: Gender shapes boys' participation too. Boys have some advantages, but they also face pressures that can limit what they feel free to do.
points: Provision and pathways: boys often have more established routes from school teams into competitive club sport, so it is easier for them to keep progressing.
Pressure to be strong and competitive: boys may feel they must excel in contact and team sports to be respected.
Ridicule: boys who choose activities labelled feminine, such as dance, may be mocked, which narrows their choices too.
notes.tip: The 2026 Higher question asks about boys, and describing two influences on boys is a Higher question. Include boys' pressures and ridicule, not only girls' barriers.

notes.b: Some barriers are practical rather than social. They affect everyone, but they can weigh more heavily on girls.
points: Time, cost and transport limit participation for all young people, especially where clubs and facilities are far from home.
For girls: safety concerns about travelling home after evening training or matches can keep them from attending.
For boys: the same time, cost and transport limits apply, but safety concerns weigh less heavily.

notes.b: Two further influences work through ideas and images rather than through facilities. Each has its own subsection, so only the main point of each is given here. There is more on these in Gender, media and body image and in Gender socialisation and its impact on participation.
points: Body image and media: idealised thin, toned and muscular bodies in advertising and social media can make young people dissatisfied with their own bodies (their body image) and deter them from activity.

Gender socialisation (learning the behaviour expected of your sex) and hegemonic ideals (the dominant, most-valued versions of masculinity and femininity): family, peers, school and media teach boys and girls what is appropriate for their sex, and these ideals steer them towards some activities and away from others.
notes.tip: Body image and media, and socialisation with hegemonic ideals, are separate subsections. Give each one short point in an influences answer and do not go into depth.

notes.b: Once the causes are known, a school can act on each one. Each measure below removes a particular barrier, so match the fix to the problem.
points: Broaden the activity offer with dance, fitness classes, aquatics (water-based activities such as swimming), outdoor pursuits and non-contact versions of games, and give students a choice, so girls who avoid competitive team games have options.
Offer girls-only or friendship-group options and non-competitive sessions alongside competitive teams, which removes the fear of being judged in mixed or competitive settings.
Provide flexible, comfortable PE kit and private, clean changing facilities, which removes self-consciousness about kit and changing.
Give girls' teams equal facility time, fixtures, coaching and recognition, shown in assemblies, on noticeboards and on social media, which removes unequal provision and invisibility.
Bring in female role models and leaders, such as older students acting as leaders and visiting female athletes and coaches, which tackles the shortage of visible women in sport.
Use student voice (asking students what they want): survey students and plan activities from the results, so provision matches what students want.
Track participation by gender to see whether the gap is closing and which measures need changing.
notes.tip: A Higher question asks you to discuss two ways a school could tackle a gender imbalance. Pick two measures and say what each does and which barrier it removes.

notes.h: Addressing the imbalance in the community
notes.b: Clubs, local bodies and national campaigns can close the gap outside school, by giving girls and women somewhere to play and by making women's sport easier to see.
points: Clubs offering girls' and women's teams at every age, with female coaches, give girls a team to join at each stage of their development.
Social, beginner and return-to-sport programmes, such as women's recreational leagues and mothers-and-daughters sessions, bring in people who would not join competitive teams.
Allocate pitches, halls and coaching fairly between girls' and boys' teams, so neither group has the better slots.
Provide safe, accessible, well-lit facilities and transport, which tackles safety concerns about travelling after dark.
Local Sports Partnership programmes (local bodies that promote sport and physical activity) targeting teenage girls reach girls through local provision.
The Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and the Camogie Association govern ladies' Gaelic football and camogie, giving girls and women their own pathway in those games.

The 20x20 campaign, launched in 2018, aims to increase the visibility of women's sport in Ireland, under the slogan 'If she can't see it, she can't be it'. Sport Ireland has a Women in Sport policy, and media coverage of women's sport adds to its visibility.
notes.tip: Exams ask how the imbalance could be addressed in the community as well as in school, so have a few of these measures ready with the problem each one solves.

keyTerms.definition: The biological characteristics, such as chromosomes, hormones and physical make-up, that define a person as male or female.
The socially constructed roles, behaviours and expectations that a society attaches to being male or female.
Taking part in physical activity or sport, recreationally or competitively, as a player, coach or leader.
Leaving sport or physical activity altogether, often during adolescence.
A physical activity that a society labels as suitable for boys or for girls.
An activity in which players do not make deliberate physical contact with each other, such as dance or individual fitness.
The teams, coaches, facilities, fixtures and funding that make participation possible.
A person whose visible example inspires others to take part or to aspire to a role in sport.
Involving students in deciding which activities are offered and how they are run.
A local partnership that delivers sport and physical activity programmes within a county or area.

questions.prompt: Examine the main influences that impact on the participation patterns of boys and girls in physical activity and sport.
questions.model: Family: parents shape activity through their own participation, what they pay for and drive to, and what they encourage. A parent may steer a son towards contact sports and a daughter towards dance, so the son gains a route into competitive sport while the daughter's options narrow. Peers: friends' choices and fear of judgement decide whether young people join or stay. A teenage girl may downplay her interest in sport because being sporty seems uncool, while for a boy sport can be central to status among peers, so he may keep playing to keep his standing. School: a range of activities dominated by competitive team games gives boys the activities they more often choose, but leaves girls who prefer non-contact activities with little choice, and boys' teams often get more of the teacher's time. Community provision: boys often have more teams, coaches and facility slots, so they can train and play more regularly, while girls' teams have fewer slots and fewer coaches. Clothing: tight or revealing kit such as leotards, athletics briefs and short skirts can make girls self-conscious and lead some of them to drop out in adolescence. Pressure on boys: boys who choose dance may be mocked, and pressure to be strong and competitive narrows the choices open to them. These influences work together, so the gap between boys and girls is social and can be narrowed by changing the conditions that produce it.

questions.prompt: Discuss two ways in which a school could address an imbalance between boys' and girls' levels of participation.
questions.model: First, broaden the activity offer and give students a choice. Dance, fitness classes, aquatics, outdoor pursuits and non-contact versions of games give girls, who more often choose non-contact and individual activity, options they will actually take up. This removes the barrier of a narrow programme dominated by competitive team games, and it keeps boys who prefer these activities engaged too. Second, provide flexible, comfortable PE kit and private, clean changing facilities. A girl who is self-conscious about tight or short kit, or who has no privacy to change, can then take part without fear of being watched or judged, so the barrier of self-consciousness is removed. The school can check whether either strategy is working by surveying students and tracking participation by gender.

questions.prompt: Explain how the clothing required in some sports can affect participation.
questions.model: Some sports require kit that is tight, short or revealing, such as swimwear, leotards, athletics briefs and short skirts. Wearing such kit can make a teenager feel exposed and self-conscious about their body, and worry about being watched or judged can lead them to avoid the activity or drop out, especially in adolescence. For example, a girl may avoid swimming lessons or athletics because she dislikes the kit she has to wear. A solution is comfortable kit that students can choose, such as tracksuit bottoms and loose tops, so they can take part without feeling exposed.
